references.text: A leper falls on his face before Jesus and asks for healing – the same humble posture shown by the Samaritan in [ref:Luk 5:12|Luke 5:12].
The woman who falls at Jesus' feet in gratitude, similarly to the Samaritan in [ref:Luk 7:36-38|Luke 7:36-38]. Both express deep humility and thankfulness at Jesus' feet.

In the parable of the Good Samaritan, it is also a Samaritan who acts rightly, unlike Jews who fail – a parallel to how here it is the Samaritan who returns and gives thanks in [ref:Luk 10:33|Luke 10:33].

Naaman, a foreign army commander, returns to the prophet Elisha after being healed of leprosy and acknowledges the God of Israel – a strong parallel to the Samaritan stranger who returns to thank Jesus in [ref:2 Kong 5:15|2 Kings 5:15].
The Jewish-Samaritan hostility is highlighted in [ref:Joh 4:9|John 4:9], making the Samaritan's gratitude even more remarkable.
The Samaritans of Sychar come to faith in Jesus in [ref:Joh 4:39-42|John 4:39-42]. Here too it is Samaritans – outsiders – who respond positively to Jesus.
The Samaritans receive the gospel with joy in [ref:Apg 8:5-8|Acts 8:5-8], pointing to the same pattern: those outside Israel receive God's grace with thankfulness.
Paul urges believers to be thankful in [ref:Kol 3:15|Colossians 3:15]. The Samaritan's spontaneous thanks to Jesus is a living example of such gratitude.
Abraham falls on his face before God in [ref:1 Mos 17:3|Genesis 17:3], a gesture of deep reverence and worship – the same posture the Samaritan takes before Jesus.
Joshua falls on his face to the ground in worship before the commander of the Lord's army in [ref:Jos 5:14|Joshua 5:14], a parallel to the Samaritan's humble kneeling at Jesus' feet.

Jesus himself comments that only this foreigner (ἀλλογενής) returned to give glory to God in [ref:Luk 17:18|Luke 17:18], underscoring the theological significance of it being a Samaritan who gave thanks.
